newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK borrowers come back.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK borrowers come back.

text.p: Asian debt markets offered up a few more Hong Kong issues on Tuesday.
Manhattan Card set a HK$400 million floating certificate of deposit issue via arrangers Chase Manhattan Asia, JP Morgan Securities Asia and Schroders Asia.

The certificates mature in five years but can be put or called on the third and fourth anniversary. They pay a margin of 45 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate and, with fees, an all-in return of 54 basis points.
The issue also can be put if Chase Manhattan Asia's share of the borrower falls below 51 percent or if Manhattan Card ceases to be a restricted licence bank in Hong Kong.
Manhattan Card last tapped the market in September 1995 with a similar issue with a five-year final maturity and puts and calls in years three and four.
In line with the trend, the latest transaction pays far less than the 1995 deal, which offered a margin of 60 basis points over HIBOR and an all-in of 70 basis points.
Bankers said Standard Chartered Bank's HK$2.0 billion FRCD launched on Monday is attracting good demand.
Syndicate managers predict that many of the other Hong Kong banks that can place LAF issues will be tapping the market soon.
Issues that are eligible to be used as collateral at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), or discount window, tend to be more attractive.
To be eligible, issues must be at least HK$1.0 billion in size and have an A-level rating from one of a number of rating agencies.
"Over the next few weeks and months, I would expect to see more LAF paper," said one syndicate manager. But he added that the number of banks and corporations that can qualify is relatively small.
Hong Kong's GE Capital, a wholly owned subsidiary of General Electric Capital Corp, formally launched its Kangaroo FRN today via lead manager Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
Also in Hong Kong, bankers said that CITIC Pacific is considering various ways of accessing longer term funding for its purchase of China Light and Power shares.
CITIC Pacific last month signed a HK$12.5 billion bridge loan with five banks to help fund the HK$16.5 billion purchase of the utility. The loan has a tenor of less than one year.
At that time, CITIC Pacific said it would consider various ways to raise longer-term funding.
"The amount needed is so large that CITIC is sure to finance in a variety of ways, perhaps including equity, loans and bonds," said a syndicate manager.
He said the company has received many unsolicited offers from banks to arrange a deal.
Rumours that the company is mulling a seven-year HK$7-8 billion term loan, a Yankee issue or both have been circulating in the market.
Bankers also said that Shanghai Industrial Holdings is expected to seek a five-year US$200 million loan facility.

Shanghai Industrial Investment Holdings, which wholly owns Shanghai Investment Holdings which in turn holds 65.1 percent of Shanghai Industrial Holdings, completed a five-year US$80 million club loan earlier this year.
In other news from Asia, the Inter-American Development Bank launched a US$1.0 billion global bond out of Tokyo this morning.
